items.name: tokens
items.title: Vendored tokens and utilities
items.description: What @fluid's components take for granted but no registry item installs: the interaction tokens, the focus ring and the scroll utilities. Without this the proximity highlight paints transparent.
items.docs: The four systems are wired once at the root: MotionConfig reducedMotion="user", ShapeProvider, SizeProvider, SurfaceProvider and TooltipProvider. What this item does NOT bring, because it's the app's decision and not the components': the background on <html>, the native scrollbars and the ColorPicker's checkerboard. If you're going to nest a theme (LoginBlock paints itself light inside a dark app), duplicate the light values' selector to `:root, .light`.

items.name: use-measured-height
items.title: useMeasuredHeight
items.description: Measures the content's real height with a ResizeObserver so it can be animated. PeekCard uses it when the tab changes.

items.name: animated-empty
items.title: AnimatedEmpty
items.description: The empty state with the anatomy of shadcn's Empty, choreographed: the figure, the title, the description and the action come in staggered, and the exit runs backwards and faster.
items.docs: The entry order comes from the composition: the block staggers its children and the header staggers its own, so reordering the JSX reorders the animation. The entry happens on its own; for the exit you have to wrap it in an <AnimatePresence mode="wait"> and give it a key per reason for the emptiness, or the text changes inside a figure that's already in place.

items.name: travel-tooltip
items.title: TravelTooltip
items.description: One tooltip shared by a group: moving from one trigger to its neighbour, it travels instead of reappearing.

items.name: inset-dialog
items.title: InsetDialog
items.description: The dialog with its content inset into a card of its own: header and footer share the frame's plane. It's the dialog base for the rest of the in-house components.
items.docs: With placement="bottom" it anchors to the floor and becomes a sheet: the motion step changes and the × is dropped. The tray goes four surface steps down instead of the card going up, so it needs the root's SurfaceProvider to know where to start from.

items.name: mobile-action-confirmation
items.title: MobileActionConfirmation
items.description: The sheet that confirms an action on a phone screen, and the sequence of steps when the action is more than one.

items.name: peek-card
items.title: PeekCard
items.description: The card with tabs that opens stuck to whatever fires it, on click or on hover.
items.docs: The registry publishes `card` compiled for Next.js: it imports next/link. Outside Next you have to swap that import for an anchor —or for your router's Link— or the build won't resolve.

items.name: calendar
items.title: RangeCalendar · DatePicker · DateTimePicker
items.description: Three faces of the same month: a stay with the band between its two ends, a single day, and a day whose second field turns the plane into the clock's three columns: hour, minutes and AM/PM.
items.docs: One implementation, three exports: `RangeCalendar` (two ends and a counter of nights), `DatePicker` (one day, and the counter says what the day is) and `DateTimePicker` (`DatePicker` with `time`, whose second field takes the plane over to three columns: the hour, the minutes and AM/PM). The subject is the answer and not the grid, so the fields (`fields`) and the presets (`presets`) turn off independently and what's left is a month to drop in a popover. Dates are plain `Date`s at local midnight and the labels come from `Intl`, so the locale is a prop and not a translation file — and a moment is one `Date` carrying the day and the hour, with the one ambiguity that a value at exactly midnight reads as an hour not yet picked. The columns are the whole clock —00 to 12, 00 to 59, and the half of the day— and what can't be picked is greyed rather than removed, the same deal the month makes with `minDate`. Which times those are comes from `timeStep` (every minute by default) plus `timeRange`, or outright from `times` in minutes from midnight. On a twelve-hour clock midnight is `00` and noon is `12`, so `12` is greyed under AM and `00` under PM: one row per hour of the day, and no two rows meaning the same moment. The two columns of numbers are captioned from `hourLabel` and `minuteLabel`, like every other visible string here. Whether the clock has twelve hours and a half-of-the-day column or twenty-four and none of it is the locale's answer, read from `Intl` — not a prop. The accent —band, endpoints, chosen hour and the field's underline— is the `--calendar-accent` variable: set it on the calendar or above it and every mark moves together; `--calendar-band` overrides the band's fill on its own, for a theme where 12% of the accent isn't enough. `minDate` defaults to today; pass `null` for a calendar that reaches backwards.

items.name: timeline
items.title: Timeline
items.description: Lo que pasó, en el orden en que pasó: hitos con su estado o un feed de actividad, con el riel dibujándose hacia abajo.
items.docs: Two shapes of the same object, and the prop is `variant`: `milestones` puts the time under the title because the row is a paragraph, `feed` puts it against the right edge because the row is a sentence. Each item draws the piece of rail below it —not the list— so an entry that arrives brings its own and `group-last` retires the one that stopped being last, with no index arithmetic and no cloning of children. State is weight and not colour (a ring, a filled dot with a halo of the interaction tokens, a hairline); colour is what `Badge` is for and it means a category. An `icon` replaces the dot: a feed says what kind of thing happened, and the state of something already done is always done. What hangs off an entry goes in `TimelineNote`, a step up with `Elevated` rather than a quote border. It renders an `<ol>`, because the order is the content.

items.name: widget
items.title: Widget
items.description: The descriptor of a view that knows how to show itself at three sizes —the board's glance, the PeekCard and the whole tab— and the tile that becomes the tab instead of opening it.
items.docs: It hangs off a WorkspaceProvider — that's who opens the tab — so without one it throws. And a widget is drawn once per screen: the layoutId that makes the move comes from its id, and two tiles of the same widget mounted at once are the same object as far as Framer is concerned, so it crosses them. That's why the tile leaves a gap while its view is the active tab: it's what lets the board stay mounted off to the side. The tile carries a header with the name and, if you pass onClose, the button that takes it off the board; what opens the widget is a surface covering the card and not a button around everything, because a button can't contain another one.

items.name: widget-drag
items.title: WidgetDragProvider
items.description: One drag for the whole shell: the context that lets a card leave one board and land in another — a tray in the panel, the board in the rail.
items.docs: Mount it above every board that has to share cards; a board that only sorts its own cells needs nothing, because `WidgetGrid` mounts a context of its own when there isn't one above. The provider routes and the boards decide: each one signs up with what it's willing to do —reorder its own cells, accept a foreign one, release one that left— and a drop is the provider calling the right pair. Nothing is removed from anywhere until the other end has said yes, so a board that takes no `onAdd`, or one that answers `false` because the payload isn't something it can hold, sends the card back. What travels between regions is a DragOverlay in a portal: a cell that left its box would be cut off by the panel's own scroll exactly when it starts crossing. A copy lands under an id the provider mints, because two cells with one id would be a collision for the sort and, when the cell holds a widget, the same object in two places for Framer; the board that receives is handed that id and adds the card under it. What the overlay draws while a copy travels goes in a LayoutGroup of its own, so the original and the copy of it in the air don't share a layoutId.

items.name: widget-card
items.title: WidgetCard
items.description: The wrapper that places something on the board: it takes the span, it signs up with the grid and it carries the drag. Whatever goes inside is not its business — a widget's tile, a figure, three lines of text.
items.docs: The dragging is @dnd-kit's: useSortable for the cell, and the context that routes it is @wabi/widget-drag's — one for a lone board, one for the whole shell when a card has to travel between regions. `WidgetGrid` is what a board wraps its cells in: it owns the arrangement, signs up with the drag and draws the outline of where a card coming from elsewhere would land. Two things are the house's and not the library's: the activator is bound on the capture phase, because a widget's tile stops pointerdown from bubbling (whatever must not start a drag says so with `data-no-drag`), and the sensors carry the house's numbers — 4px of travel for a pointer, a 350ms hold for a finger, so the board still scrolls on a phone. A grid that neither sorts nor lets a card leave draws cards that never call the hook: no node registered, no tab stop, no cursor promising a gesture. `data` is what a card carries for the board that takes it. `copy` decides whether the original stays: by default a card moves —it lands on the other board and leaves the one it came from— and with `copy` it's a source instead, so the original stays where it was and what lands is one of its own under a new id (`name-copy`, and a number after that if there's one already). Sorting inside its own board is unchanged, because there's nothing there to duplicate into. What travels is the card's `data` and what it draws, not the React state inside its children: a copy mounts fresh, so anything it has to be born with goes in `data`.

items.name: widget-board
items.title: WidgetBoard
items.description: The grid of cells: a size ladder from 1x1 to 2x2, layout driven by a container query, drag and drop to rearrange it, and the AnimatedEmpty when there are none.
items.docs: Meant to live beside the panel as a region of the shell, not inside a tab. It measures its container and not the window: the layout comes from @container, so in a narrow rail it falls into one column and with width it shows the size ladder. It doesn't own the list: it reports through onWidgetClose and whoever uses it drops the widget from `widgets`. Without that callback the tiles show no close button. With onClose it draws a button reading «Close» at the top right, whether the board is full or empty: the board doesn't own its place and only reports. Every cell is a `WidgetCard` —dnd-kit underneath— so the board is rearranged by dragging wherever it takes an `onReorder`: it keeps the arrangement while the hand is moving and hands back the ids when the card lands, and whoever owns the list sorts it. With `onAdd` it also becomes a destination for cards dragged in from another board —returning `false` refuses one— and with `onRemove` its own cards can leave; both need a shared @wabi/widget-drag provider above the two boards. Cells that aren't widgets go in as `WidgetCard` children: anything with an id can share the grid. With `copy` the cards it builds for its widgets are sources rather than pieces: the original stays and a copy lands on the other board, which is what turns a board into a palette — and `onRemove` never fires, because nothing leaves. Cards passed as children carry their own `copy`. The list scrolls and the region around it doesn't: the header stays put and the grid moves, with no scrollbar at all. `scroll-fade` is the cue — the cells dissolve towards whichever edge still has more — and `scrollbar-hide` drops the track, because one pinned to the edge of a column this narrow either rides over a tile or eats the air that keeps the grid centred. Same treatment as the WorkspacePanel's tab row.

items.name: widget-rail
items.title: WidgetRail
items.description: The widget rail beside the panel. It brings no handle of its own: it's resized from outside, with the handle it exposes through controlRef, and the panel never drops below 55% of the screen — before stopping, the drag folds the sidebar.
items.docs: It hangs off a SidebarProvider — it needs to be able to fold it when the drag hits the limit — and it stands to the right of the panel: it measures its previous sibling in the DOM to know how much the two are splitting, so it goes after it. It isn't grabbed by the edge: through controlRef it exposes a handle with beginResize(event), nudge(delta) and step, and whoever resizes is the control that uses it — in this app, a button in the panel's bar. Through the `preview` prop it shows something else instead of the board — a LateralPreview, usually — and the board comes back when you remove it; while it lasts the rail widens by 140px, the preview rests against its borders, and if there's no room for that the sidebar folds. It reports through onResizingChange while the drag lasts. If the ceiling falls below a widget's width, the rail hides instead of showing a strip. onWidgetReorder, onWidgetAdd, onWidgetRemove and onBoardClose are passed straight through to the board — with the last three, a widget can be dragged in from a tray in the panel and back out again: the rail is the place and doesn't decide what's shown in it.

items.name: lateral-preview
items.title: LateralPreview
items.description: The glance at a single thing in the side rail —a conversation, a profile, a board of numbers—, with its fixed header, its scrolling body and its footer for opening the whole thing.
items.docs: It's the WidgetBoard's counterpart and takes its same place: the board says how everything is going, the preview says what this is. It doesn't know what it's showing — there's one frame and whoever uses it supplies the body, with PreviewGroup, PreviewRow, PreviewStat and PreviewMessage or with anything else. It fills its container's height: in the rail that's the whole column.

items.name: preview-context
items.title: PreviewProvider
items.description: The provider that gives the rail what it has to preview from anywhere in the app: usePreview().show() wherever it's needed.
items.docs: Same problem and same solution as workspace-context: the rail is drawn on one side of the shell and whatever asks for a preview lives anywhere else. LateralPreview knows nothing about it — it takes its content through props and works just as well on its own, with no provider.

items.name: filter-menu
items.title: FilterMenu
items.description: The two-level filter menu: a view's attributes and, inside each one, its values, with no side submenu.

items.name: workspace-panel
items.title: WorkspacePanel
items.description: The content frame with connected tabs that sits next to the sidebar, with the active tab's plane on a single sliding layer.
items.docs: It calls useSidebar(), so it has to hang off a SidebarProvider — without one it throws. It doesn't own its tabs: it takes `tabs` and reports through `onTabClose`. If you want to open them from anywhere in the app, add @wabi/workspace-context. The `controls` prop is the far right of the bar, outside the scrolling row: that's where the panel's controls go. The `lifted` prop raises its shadow two steps: it's there so an external handle —the widget rail's— can say the panel is about to be resized.

items.name: workspace-context
items.title: WorkspaceProvider
items.description: The provider that gives WorkspacePanel its tabs from anywhere in the app: WorkspaceOutlet where it's drawn and useWorkspace().openTab() wherever it's needed.

items.name: window-controls
items.title: WindowControls
items.description: The bar that drives the window and the sidebar — full screen, floating window, side panel.
items.docs: The sidebar button calls useSidebar(), so that part has to hang off a SidebarProvider. It takes children —your own TravelTooltipItems, inside the same travelling tooltip— and `more={false}` to leave the browser menu out when the bar is made only of the app's controls.

items.name: login-block
items.title: LoginBlock
items.description: The complete sign-in screen: the brand plane on the left, the form and the providers on the right. The layout comes from a container query, not from a viewport breakpoint.
items.docs: It paints itself light or dark on its own by putting the class on its own root, without touching the <html>. For that to work, the theme's light values have to be declared in `:root, .light` and not only in `:root`. Inside the block you can't use a single `dark:` utility: the variant is defined as `&:is(.dark *)` and would match anyway.
